cards.explanation: The oath was this: “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” The men of Israel swore it at Mizpah, and I think they had no idea how much trouble one sentence could cause. Say a thing out loud and mean it, and you can't stuff it back in the bowl. Hold onto that oath, friends, because everything else in this passage bends around it.

What the people ask is why one tribe is missing from Israel. They cry out, “Why, O LORD God of Israel, has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” Notice they take the question straight to God, and they do it weeping. The tribe that's missing is Benjamin, and the people feel the hole it leaves.

The answer is death. The oath said that “…anyone who failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death.” That's a heavy promise to make, and it matters because the people are about to check who didn't show. A solemn oath is no small thing in Israel.

The answer is wives. They ask, “What should we do about wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage?” See the knot? They grieve for Benjamin and want the survivors to have wives, but their own oath is standing in the doorway. It's like being locked out with the keys sitting on the kitchen counter.

The answer is Jabesh-gilead. The text says, “…no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the assembly.” When the people were counted, none of its residents were there. A head count is the kind of thing nobody can talk their way around. What comes next is heavy, so I'll just say that plainly.

The answer is four hundred. The men found “…four hundred young women who had not had relations with a man…” and brought them to the camp at Shiloh in the land of Canaan. It's a sober part of the story, and I think it deserves a quiet moment. Keep that number handy, friends, because it turns out not to be enough.

The answer is False. The Benjamites were given the women spared from Jabesh-gilead, “But there were not enough women for all of them.” So some of the men were still without wives. That's why the elders have to come up with something else.

The answer is heirs. The elders say, “There must be heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out.” A tribe only lasts if there's a next generation to carry it. That's what they're trying to protect.

The answer is a feast to the LORD in Shiloh. The elders say, “there is a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh…” They give the spot such careful directions that you could find it with your eyes closed. And the text calls it yearly, so it comes around every year.

The answer is the vineyards. The elders tell the Benjamites, “Go, hide in the vineyards and watch.” Rows of vines make a decent hiding place, and the Benjamites are told to wait there until the moment comes. It's a plan with a lot of waiting in it.

The answer is the daughters of Shiloh coming out to dance. The Benjamites are told, “When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to perform their dances…” they are to come out of the vineyards. So the whole plan hangs on watching and waiting for that one moment. A hiding place is only as good as your patience.

The answer is False. The elders tell each man to “…catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.” Nobody is told to stay and settle at Shiloh. The plan points them straight back home.

The answer is give. The elders say, “Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.” Their reasoning leans on that one word, because the oath was about giving a daughter. It's a lot of weight to put on a single verb, friends.

The answer is True. The Benjamites did as instructed, and the text says they “…went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their cities, and settled in them.” After everything this tribe went through, I'm glad to see it back on its feet. The tribe has a place to live again, friends.

The answer is back to his own tribe and inheritance. The text says, “…each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance.” After all that weeping, fighting and plotting, everyone heads back to their own place. Nothing says they stay.
